articles.title: New AJK government’s task
articles.content: DESPITE hurdles, doubts, speculation, a protest movement and delayed polls on seven out of 45 directly contested Legislative Assembly seats, the task ofinstalling a new government in Azad Jammu and Kashmirhas finally been accomplished. There had been serious questions about the fairness of the elections. Thebitterest criticismwas from the PPP, the PML-N’s ally in the national parliament. Even the AJK prime minister’s election was not without controversy. Barrister Iftikhar Gillani was not selected or even recommended as a candidate for the office by the PML-N parliamentary party of the AJK assembly; rather, he was picked by the president of PML-N Pakistan. The choice was resented by some senior party leaders, including Shah Ghulam Qadir, the party president in AJK, who boycotted the assembly session that elected the PM. The key objection to Mr Gillani’s election as PM was not his relative inexperience compared to veterans such as former PM Raja Farooq Haider or former speaker Shah Ghulam Qadir but the mode of his election as an assembly member. He had lost his seat — the Muzaffarabad constituency, LA-29 — to his PPP rival in the election by over 3,000 votes. Still, he returned to the assembly on a seat reserved for technocrats. There is no legal bar to the eligibility of a member who is defeated in the general election and subsequently elected on a reserved seat to seek the PM’s office. But many politicians believe that a PM should win the confidence of his constituency before seeking the coveted position. However, despite a turbulent electoral phase that had been ongoing for some months, the new government and PM have assumed office in AJK. Given the PML-N’s clear majority in the assembly, the election of a new AJK president of the PML-N’s choice will likely be a formality. The most important question, however, concerns the new government’s agenda and how far it can overcome the most serious challenges ever faced by an AJK government. A negotiated solution must be found for all contentious issues. In view of the circumstances surrounding the entire electoral process, the foremost challenge before the new government and the PM is to establish the government’s moral and performance legitimacy, even if one accepts its electoral legitimacy. Opening the lines of communication with theoutlawedJoint Awami Action Committee, engaging with the saner elements within the organisation, and convincing them to abandon the agitation will be the government’s first major test. If successful, it will pave the way for legitimacy of performance. Although the outlawed JAAC can justifiably be blamed for several irresponsible and anti-state utterances and actions, the fact remains that the defunct organisation has a sizeable following, especially in Poonch division, where, despite its best efforts, including organising phased polls, the AJK Election Commission could not hold elections in seven out of 11 constituencies. A sizeable crowd has been staging a sit-in for almost three months, partly paralysing civic life and links with the rest of AJK and Pakistan. The confrontation and deaths of some agitators and law-enforcement personnel have polarised Kashmiris not only in AJK but also among the diaspora. This confrontation has damaged goodwill and the moral standing of authorities in AJK and Pakistan. The situation, therefore, must be defused immediately and a negotiated solution found for the contentious issues. It was unreasonable, arguably, for the outlawed JAAC to insist on immediately abolishing the 12 AJK assembly seats reserved for Kashmiri refugees settled in various parts of Pakistan. This demand became even more absurd after the AJK Supreme Court ruled in June that the legislative assembly seats reserved for refugees were constitutionally protected and could not be abolished through executive action or street protests. However, it is also true that the constitutional reforms on the allocation of seats between refugees from the occupied Kashmir valley and Jammu need to be seriously considered, along with the election procedure. The election to the AJK assembly from various parts of Pakistan is generally heavily influenced by the federal and provincial governments during the poll cycle. Now that the new legislative assembly is in place, it should seriously initiate deliberations on constitutional reforms. In general, the outlawed JAAC’s demands are not unreasonable and are mostly directed at welfare measures and better governance. For example, the demand for a smaller cabinet and the abolition of lavish facilities for elected representatives and senior bureaucrats should be sympathetically considered, alongside calls for roads, tunnels, bridges, safe drinking water, and preventing development budgetary funds from lapsing. Demanding empowered local governments and elected students’ unions is also fair. These are not just JAAC demands, but what every Kashmiri and also many in Pakistan demand. The new government can build on the previous government’s acceptance of most demands and begin implementing the points already agreed upon. The new PM may begin by forming a smaller cabinet and cutting back on unnecessary protocol and unproductive spending. If tangible steps are taken early for better governance, a solid foundation may be laid for broader reconciliation. In the long term, both the federal government in Pakistan and the AJK government should consider granting AJK the same rights and privileges enjoyed by the four provinces. The same goes for Gilgit-Baltistan. A constitutional way should be found to provide interim representation to AJK and GB in federal institutions such as parliament, the Council of Common Interests, the National Economic Council and the water regulator Irsa, without compromising our position on the Kashmir dispute. The denial of these rights over the last 80 years has become a major source of grievance. The writer is president of the Pakistan-based think tank Pildat.
articles.author: Ahmed Bilal Mehboob

articles.title: Shame and shamelessness
articles.content: “You must never lose your sense of shame. If one is past all shame, what is one fit for? One lives like a bird in moult, shedding virtues like plumes all pointing down to hell” — Wolfram von Eschenbach (German poet.) I’VE been wrestling with this idea — the essentiality of shame for retaining humanity — for some time now. But I am reminded of it every time I read in the news about how one judge or the other has, again, successfully continued Imaan Mazari and Hadi Chattha’s perverseincarceration. The novelShamepresents another take on the idea. While acknowledging its necessity, it argues shame is never truly lost. It is suppressed, it is unacknowledged, it is transferred to others, but it invariably re-emerges, nay erupts, mutated into manifestations of violence and tyranny throughout society. Surviving in Pakistan (but, more specifically, thriving in Pakistan) demands the suppression of shame. Being more fortunate, we suppress the shame of a cruel and rapacious system built to profit the powerful by exploiting the powerless. As Muslims, we suppress our shame at how we steadily criminalise the very existence of our minorities and force them to leap through ever-higher hoops to earn their right to live. As citizens, we suppress the shame of a state that has long abandoned any pretence to being representative and casually disappears dissidents. As lawyers, we suppress the shame of a legal system indifferent to justice and riddled with cowardice and venality. We suppress the shame, not only from fear of the consequences of speaking or acting, but so we can live with ourselves. There are a few, however, who feel the sting of shame more sharply. They speak, and act, while we watch. They carry the burden of our collective shame and expiate it. There are a few who carry the burden of our collective shame and expiate it. Imaan and Hadi belong on that list. One might not subscribe to all their opinions. One might think them misguided in some of the causes they choose to advocate. And, while ensconced in the quiet safety of one’s living room, one can disagree with their or, more particularly, her manner of articulation. But while we may not possess the courage to emulate them, do we lack even the shame to admire them? This January, Judge Afzal Manjoka sentenced the couple to prison for 17 years. As per the judgement, Imaan’s crime was sending six tweets. In one, she posted a picture of Mahrang Baloch raising a victory sign and encouraged the public to raise their voice against fake encounters, enforced disappearances and killings in Balochistan. In another, she said innocents kept in illegal detention and torture cells were also victims — just like those targeted in terrorist attacks. In a third tweet, she said state repression in Balochistan was making the insurgency worse. In a fourth, she argued that reports about anti-terrorist operations by security officials in Balochistan had lost credibility. Two of her tweets were about KP. In the first, she said “we said never forget but acted like nothing happened. The terrorist who had our children slaughtered was set free by the state. The disastrous good Taliban vs bad Taliban policy continues even today”. Presumably, she was referring to the TTP’s former spokesperson, Ehsanullah Ehsan, who initially surrendered and was detained in a military safe-house but later ‘escaped’ and claimed to be living the expatriate’s dream in Turkiye. Notably, the parents of the 147 children in theArmy Public School massacreearlier raised the same grievance in their petition before the Supreme Court. Her second tweet condemned the forced disappearance of Ghazi Amanullah, brother of PTM leader Manzoor Pashteen, and argued the state was targeting peaceful dissidents and their families. As I said earlier, one might object to the tenor of some of her speech. But the content? Who seriously disagrees that the good Taliban, bad Taliban strategy we’ve followed on and off in Afghanistan and Pakistan for three decades has, on each occasion, come back to bite us? Or that decades of the state’s undiscriminating repression in Balochistan has only fuelled the insurgency? But even if you disagree, and are a genuine adherent of the ‘Pindi knows best’ philosophy, do you reckon people expressing the contrary view should be convicted of terrorism and jailed for 17 years? Poor Hadi, of course, didn’t even tweet anything himself. The judgement accuses him, however, of retweeting four of Imaan’s tweets. Unstated in the judgement (but imprudently expressed by Chief Justice Sarfaraz Dogar in an earlier, unrelated, case) is his true crime: being a Pakistani man who cannot control his own wife. But my question is not to Judge Manjoka, nor about how closely his judgement of Jan 24 hews to the narrative expressed in the press conference held on Jan 6 by a security official accusing Imaan of being “a lawyer for terrorists” and “a foreign agent”. My question is to everyone who wears a judicial robe: how is it possible to witness the travesty of Imaan and Hadi’s trial, the breach of every principle of due process, the utter frivolity of the charges against them, the draconian punishments awarded to them, and not feel an outpouring of shame at one’s own helplessness? It is to everyone who wears a black coat. How can one belong to a profession committed to upholding the rule of law yet observe the presidents of the Supreme Court Bar and Islamabad High Court Bar (belonging to the Asma Jahangir group, no less!) defending these convictions; and witness the failure of the majority of bars to rise to the defence of their own, without feeling the sharp sting of shame? The question is about the nature of shame itself. What happens to a society forced to live without it? The writer is a member of the Pakistan Bar Council.
articles.author: Salahuddin Ahmed

articles.title: ‘Kindly adjust’
articles.content: ‘KINDLY adjust’ is a peculiarly South Asian expression. It means tolerating inconvenience or accommodating what is not quite right. While courteous, it captures the relationship between citizens and the institutions that govern them. When electricity disappears, arrange a generator. When water is scarce or unsafe, call a tanker and install a filter. When schools, hospitals, roads or air disappoint, pay privately, reroute, stay indoors or stretch the household budget. In other words: kindly adjust. Pakistanis have become exceptionally good at adjusting. What we proudly call resilience is often the ability of citizens to compensate privately for the failure of public institutions. Those with money buy electricity, water, education, healthcare, security and protection. The middle class stretches to follow; the poor endure or leave for work abroad. But there are limits to adjustment. The recent deaths of newborn babies in a fire at Islamabad’s premier government hospital brought this home with unbearable force. When something as fundamental as the safety of infants in a public hospital cannot be assured, institutional failure is no longer an inconvenience. It becomes a matter of life and death. Pakistan’s problem is that government too often mistakes programmes, budgets, authorities and committees for real delivery and measurable achievement. Education is counted in schools, teachers and budgets, not whether children learn. Healthcare is counted in hospitals and beds, not outcomes and safety. Environmental policy represents aspiration while citizens face unreliable supply, polluted air and untreated waste. The first adjustment, therefore, must come from government itself. Public institutions should be judged by outcomes. Every major public service should publish standards: learning outcomes, hospital safety, healthcare availability, affordable and reliable utilities including safe municipal water and garbage collection. Performance against them should be public. When government fails, citizens pay through illness, lost productivity and private expenditure. Resilience has become an excuse for poor governance. Accountability must match authority. Pakistan has many officials empowered to approve, regulate, inspect and prohibit, but too few who are clearly answerable when things go wrong. Each disaster is followed by an inquiry, suspension or committee, yet real learning remains elusive. Serious failures should automatically trigger independent investigation. Regulators need professional leadership. Senior appointments should carry measurable objectives. Authority without consequence encourages indifference. Government also needs capability. Career civil servants remain indispensable, but a modern economy needs specialisation, lateral entry, merit-based appointments, fixed tenures and measurable objectives. The aim is to combine institutional experience with specialist knowledge and managerial competence. Government must also simplify procedures, reduce overlapping responsibilities and give managers enough authority to be accountable. Pakistan needs better people in government, and systems in which good people can perform. The state must also reconsider what it tries to do. Pakistan has a government that is simultaneously too large and too weak: involved in too many activities, yet frequently unable to deliver basics. It should do fewer essential things much better at lower cost, which would also reduce the burden of taxes on the narrow formal sector. Another adjustment is to take government closer to citizens. Pakistan devolved authority to the provinces under the 18th Amendment but largely failed to complete the journey. Neighbourhood water, garbage collection, primary schools, local roads and district hospitals require empowered elected local governments with predictable resources and clear accountability. None of this absolves citizens or businesses of responsibility. Citizens cannot demand good services while evading taxes, stealing electricity, encroaching on public land, bribing officials or ignoring regulations. Businesses cannot demand predictable policy while seeking exemptions, protection and preferential treatment. Citizens should pay fair taxes and obey reasonable laws. Businesses should compete rather than seek privilege. For too long we have treated people’s capacity to cope as a national virtue. But resilience has become an excuse for poor governance. As Pakistan approaches its 80th year, citizens should not be expected to continue to adjust to shortages, inflation, insecurity, poor services, weak regulation and repeated economic crises. The state must deliver through declared standards, competent management and strong accountability.The elite who can afford to bypass state services should join the masses in demanding delivery. The writer is a former CEO of Unilever Pakistan and of the Pakistan Business Council.
articles.author: Ehsan Malik

articles.title: A horse and a man
articles.content: IN Pakistan, English-language newspapers are mostly read in the big cities. Even there, many readers skim the headlines. Nowadays, the news is mostly bad and hope is hard to find, so, it is safe to assume, many do not go much further. News about small villages, places where life is not determined by the vagaries of urbanised existence, is often where city dwellers do not look. There are important stories in these places as well. It is in one of these spots that you would have found a story about a man and a horse published a few days ago. According to the story, a 45-year-old herdsman named Mukhtar used to graze his cattle in fields in the jurisdiction of the Yousufwala police station in Sahiwal. Mukhtar’s life was spent among his animals, including a beloved mare that he had raised with affection. It was probably the sort of life difficult to imagine for those of us who spend our days surrounded by other human beings, traffic, Wi-Fi and all the rest of it. The simplicity of Mukhtar’s life was interrupted when his relatives insisted that the mare be handed over to them. Despite Mukhtar’s opposition, his parents handed it over. Distraught, Mukhtar climbed an electricity pole and grabbed live wires. He died on the spot. His family, the same people who had been the cause of Mukhtar’s anguish, did not want a postmortem. No one knows what happened to the mare. Many city dwellers who read such a story would consider it a tale of rural foolishness. Imagine caring so much for an animal as to take such action. Living away from animals, other than the crows, stray cats and dogs that eke out an existence in Pakistani cities, such affection for an animal is anathema. Smug as they may be, their conclusion is the wrong one. While it is undoubtedly tragic that a man chose to take his life for any reason, the fact that he did so for a horse should not be the subject of disdain or ridicule. It should, in fact, remind us of the extremely close relationship humans can have with other creatures. One casualty of urban existence has been the loss of this understanding and, with it, an appreciation of a whole non-human universe. The assumption animals are unfeeling creatures is wrong. Horses have played central roles in human lives for millennia. Humans have been domesticating horses for thousands of years. People living on the Eurasian steppes of what is now Kazakhstan first tamed them and began a story that continues to this day. Nearly all domesticated horses, including the mare whose loss led Mukhtar to take his own life, descend from a lineage belonging to the Volga-Don region around 4,200 years ago. After this, human life transformed, making long distance travel and different kinds of human settlements possible. For thousands of years, they have been a primary means of human movement, becoming entrenched in human culture. Beyond utility, however, horses are special because they are intelligent creatures that can detect and respond to human emotions. In our human-centred world, we rely on verbal communication to tell each other how we feel, what we want, what we fear and so on. As a writer, I would definitely endorse the significance of words, but it is also true that our overreliance on them often blinds us to so many non-verbal sources of information and communication that can be far more accurate and honest. This is where horses play a special role. Studies have found that horses can read human facial expressions and body language. One study found that horses could distinguish between pictures of people with angry and happy expressions. They found that horses looking at pictures of anger produced greater stress reactions. Other studies have shown that horses can remember the emotional state of a hum-an from a single encounter. Naturally, then, horses can have close emotional connections with those who take care of them. A phenomenon called emotional contagion or synchrony occurs when horses mirror the emotional state of their caretakers. This means that if a horse’s handler is happy, the horse is likely to be happy too and when the handler is stressed the horse is likely to respond in the same way. In simple terms, horses are tied deeply and emotionally to the people who look after them. Mukhtar’s death by suicide in Yousafwala is a tragedy. His anguish, however, is understandable. We ignore animal feelings because we do not believe in them. Someone who takes care of a horse knows that the assumption that they are stupid, unfeeling creatures is wrong. Someone like Mukhtar would know this. It is easy to be smug and imagine that rural folk are simple-minded and animals are unfeeling. Our inclination to do so reveals more about us than it does about them. The writer is an attorney teaching constitutional law and political philosophy.
articles.author: Rafia Zakaria

articles.title: Bond revival
articles.content: PAKISTAN has raised a record $3bn in itssingle largest international capital market transactionthrough a dual-tranche Eurobond sale that drew nearly $6bn in total orders. When international investors offer to lend a country almost twice what it is asking for and are willing to do so for as long as 10 years, they are betting that Pakistan will still be solvent, still servicing its debt, and still worth holding paper on a decade from now. That bet placed by a widespread group of institutional buyers gives yet another positive spin to the economic revival story told by the government. Two years after the country was on the verge of default, that is no mean achievement. Some practical gains from this stand out: a boost to reserves, a fresh pricing benchmark, and less reliance on bilateral rollovers. Locking in money for 5.5 and 10 years, rather than the shorter rollovers that have dominated Pakistan’s external financing in recent years, pushes out the point at which this debt has to be refinanced. Followingrecent rating upgrades, this is the kind of market validation the country needed. None of that should be mistaken for cheap money, though. The coupon rates — almost equal to returns the government is paying on Roshan Digital deposits — are real, high rates in a hard currency Pakistan cannot print and is struggling to earn. For context, when Islamabad last issued dollar bonds in 2021, it borrowed five-year money at 5.875pc and 10-year money at 7.375pc. In other words, this deal costs more than the last comparable one did. Part of that gap can be attributed to international factors: global dollar rates have stayed higher for longer since the Fed’s tightening cycle, so every sovereign borrower, not just Pakistan, is paying more than it would have three or four years ago. But part of it is also Pakistan-specific. Investors are still charging a risk premium that an investment-grade country would not pay. That does not mean Pakistan has borrowed badly. It is just that the current ratings can only do so much in the prevailing market. Comparing Eurobond coupons across countries can be tricky because a rate that looks high for one issuer can be a bargain for another, once credit rating, tenor and the global rate environment are accounted for. Judged against peers of similar credit standing, Pakistan’s pricing sits towards the upper end of the range, which aligns with where the rating agencies currently place it: not investment grade, but no longer treated as a basket case either. The more useful test of this deal will come later: whether Pakistan can return to the market in a year or two and borrow at a lower cost than it did with this issue will be the real test. It will determine if the confidence on display is durable.
articles.author: Editorial

articles.title: Data theft
articles.content: AT least the government is not trying to cover it up. That, perhaps, is the only silver lining in the alarming scandal that has just come to light. We know now, straight from the horse’s mouth, that the fingerprint-based biometric verification system — supposedly built to protect citizens’ digital identities — has been thoroughly compromised. The minister of state for interior now casually dismisses it as “outdated”. Scammers have reportedly enjoyed access to supposedly secure locations, such as airports, driving licence centres, passport offices, and possibly even Nadra, to physically steal citizens’ fingerprint data. And the crisis goes deeper. In a recent meeting of the National Assembly Standing Committee on Interior, state officials admitted that scammers continue to operate with impunity despite the blocking of 18.2m illegal SIM cards over the past two and a half years. By blaming “loopholes” in the SIM issuance system and banking channels for giving criminals free rein to commit financial fraud, the state has admitted to a massive breach of public trust. No wonder citizens simply do not trust the authorities to guarantee their safety.  It must be asked: what have the authorities been doing? Given the scale of the crisis, one would expect dedicated, multi-agency taskforces to be actively dismantling these fraudulent networks. Instead, it appears the relevant regulators — the State Bank, the PTA, the National Cybercrime Investigation Authority, and Nadra — have been operating in their own silos. Now that a stakeholder committee has finally been directed to formulate practical legislative and technical measures, the outcome must be a centralised cybersecurity framework. Pakistan and its citizenry cannot afford another bureaucratic talking shop that hums and haws while yet another crisis continues to metastasise. Further, the authorities’ sudden push to collect even more intrusive personal identification data, such as facial and iris scans, must be met with severe scrutiny from legislators. They must demand detailed assurances on exactly how this new data will be secured to ensure that the glaring mistakes of the past are not repeated. There must also be consequences for the breaches that have already occurred. Before the state’s requests for more resources to “strengthen the system” can be taken seriously, those responsible for the existing negligence must be held accountable for the financial losses already incurred by the citizenry. Anything less glosses over the scale of the negligence.
articles.author: Editorial
